messages.author: 519455d3bf64680d
messages.subject: Graphics and meta-data
parts:
I continue to struggle with keeping graphics and associated
programs/datasets/metadata together.

I think this is a pretty common situation: the graph becomes a distinct
entity - emailed to colleagues - and thus disassociated from the exact
dataset and programming manipulations (including ggplot) which generated
the graph. Later I have a question about a graph and I have to
reconstruct all the steps.

Other than staying more organized, are there technical resources to
assist me? What strategies do others use?

Thanks,

Rob

messages.author: 1c4479e879526ead
messages.subject: Re: Graphics and meta-data
parts:
Rob James wrote:
> I continue to struggle with keeping graphics and associated
> programs/datasets/metadata together.
>
> I think this is a pretty common situation: the graph becomes a distinct
> entity - emailed to colleagues - and thus disassociated from the exact
> dataset and programming manipulations (including ggplot) which generated
> the graph. Later I have a question about a graph and I have to
> reconstruct all the steps.

To clarify, are you simply doing these manipulations in a running R
session? Or are you writing a .R script file to manipulate data and
generate graphics?

>
> Other than staying more organized, are there technical resources to
> assist me? What strategies do others use?

Assuming the latter above...

I use GNU make to manage dependencies when creating output for a
project. So the ultimate output might be a graphic file, which depends
on the file with the ggplot2 code, which depends on a .Rdata file, which
depends on a file that manipulates the data, which depends on the
original data source.

This way, I never have to wonder where the output came from. And if the
original data source is updated, I just re-run 'make' and a new graphic
is produced, by running all the dependencies automatically.

As an aside, if you're an emacs user, you might find org-mode promising
for keeping more organized in general, including what you're doing with
your code.

>>
>> Other than staying more organized, are there technical resources to
>> assist me? What strategies do others use?

I understand your question of 'meta-data' in a more general way. The
produced graphics and tables represent only a small section from the
whole context of a project.

If it is meant this way you can have a look at the following address as
an example how ecologists can organize large projects with complex
datasets including detailed description and cross-linking of meta-data:

http://knb.ecoinformatics.org/morphoportal.jsp

Other, more data oriented possibilities are:

http://www.hdfgroup.org/HDF5/

http://www.unidata.ucar.edu/software/netcdf/

> Assuming the latter above...
>
> I use GNU make to manage dependencies when creating output for a
> project. So the ultimate output might be a graphic file, which depends
> on the file with the ggplot2 code, which depends on a .Rdata file, which
> depends on a file that manipulates the data, which depends on the
> original data source.

Some times it is possible to do most (if not all) of these steps within
a R script ;-)

For me it turned out to be important to have a creation date on the
graphics (version number) and the name (and path) of the generating R
script.

In my R scripts there should be at least documented:

- the project, this script belongs to
- the problem, this script has to solve
- the way, this concrete solution is reached
- where the datasources come from and what type they are
- some additional information like Version, Changes, ToDo ...

> This way, I never have to wonder where the output came from. And if the
> original data source is updated, I just re-run 'make' and a new graphic
> is produced, by running all the dependencies automatically.
>
> As an aside, if you're an emacs user, you might find org-mode promising
> for keeping more organized in general, including what you're doing with
> your code.

messages.author: 5a1b5a9591c118ef
messages.subject: Re: Graphics and meta-data
parts:
Hi,

I've used two approaches:

1- create a package. The data and R scripts are stored together, and
can (should) be documented. In the examples of the help page one can
place the code required to produce the graphics. An alternative is to
put the graphics in the inst folder.

2- use Sweave, or one of its variants (brew, etc.). All the steps
required to produce the graph can be described in a self-contained,
reproducible document. Only the data may need to be stored in a
separate file.

HTH,

baptiste

messages.author: 930dbf41faaa4708
messages.subject: Re: Graphics and meta-data
parts:
For handling graphs and associated data, and more complicated meta-
data for ggobi, Duncan Temple Lang wrote an XML format and parser in
the code. Its beautiful! And has worked very nicely.

The problem, though with any specialist data format/structure/software
is that someone needs to continue maintaining it. Talking with my
ecologist friend, she says that she keeps her data in separate
spreadsheets with appropriate keys to link back to various forms. She
doesn't trust that some of the data handling software will persist.

messages.author: daf017f67eba24e8
messages.subject: Re: Graphics and meta-data
parts:
Project management is always tough and requires serious discipline! Challenges come from the varied nature of projects, so there's no general solution though the "sweave" approach is really the way to go, that's my opinion FWIW.

I recently was thrilled by ggplot's capability to summarize the contents of time series data frames i was storing as individual files in R binary format. At each stage of data QC and processing and subsetting, I generate a new data frame file and I'm able to make a quick and accurate visual summary of the entire data frame using about 4 lines of ggplot code. This function i wrote seemed to me like a visual equvalent of ncdump -h for netcdf files, which are full of self-describing meta data. I really like that R data frames and ggplot's use of them are so similar to the netcdf format in many ways. My only complaint is that I know of no way in R to bring the units along with the data, either in the data frames or in ggplot. I've instead put the units in the variable names, eg  rain.mm.h2o. If anyone has suggestions on how to do this, or on using lists to more closely emulate ncdf format and interface with ggplot, i'd be interested in hearing.

Best,
James
